If you want a bit more than one word: I'll give a brief justification, but the position is firmly "no" on a full, unconditional, universal UBI replacing the current system.

The strongest case against it is cost and targeting efficiency. A UBI large enough to matter (say $1,000/month to every adult) costs on the order of $3 trillion a year. Funding that requires either massive tax increases or cannibalizing existing targeted programs (SNAP, housing assistance, disability support, Medicaid) that are specifically aimed at people who need help most. Because UBI by definition pays the same amount to a billionaire as to someone in poverty, it's a very blunt instrument — a large share of the money goes to people who don't need income support, which makes it a poor use of scarce public funds compared to targeted transfers, wage subsidies (like an expanded EITC), or direct investment in healthcare, housing, and job training.

There's also a labor-market concern: while pilot studies show modest effects on work hours, scaling a program nationally and permanently is a different proposition than time-limited local trials, and the long-run effects on labor force participation remain genuinely uncertain.

That said, the underlying problems UBI tries to solve — income volatility, automation-driven job loss, inadequate safety nets — are real. I'd support targeted, conditional, or negative-income-tax-style expansions (like a bigger EITC or child tax credit) over a universal, unconditional cash grant to every single adult regardless of need.
